title: Giving Reports Standard
summary: Reporting is part of completing the work. Accurate, timely reports must reach the appropriate leader and channel so the right people know what was done, what happened, and what needs to happen next.

sections.title: The Standard
paragraphs: At Zura Spa, reporting is part of completing the work.

A task, session, assignment, incident, observation, concern, or responsibility is not always considered complete simply because the physical action has been carried out. Where another person needs to know the outcome, the appropriate report must also be given.

Every therapist is expected to provide accurate, timely, relevant, and professional reports concerning matters that affect clients, tasks, standards, team members, stock, equipment and property, service quality, incidents and mistakes, operational progress, and management decisions.
Reports should be communicated to the appropriate leader and, where required, posted on the appropriate Zura Spa WhatsApp wall/group/channel.
DO THE TASK → REPORT COMPLETION → ALLOW REVIEW → RESPOND TO FEEDBACK → CLOSE THE TASK
A TASK IS NOT FULLY COMPLETE IF THE PEOPLE WHO NEED TO KNOW IT IS COMPLETE HAVE NOT BEEN INFORMED.

sections.title: 1. Why Reporting Matters
paragraphs: Reporting gives management and the team visibility.

Without reporting, a therapist may know that something has been done while everyone else continues to wonder: Has it been done? Was it done correctly? Is anything still pending? Was there a problem? Does someone need to review it? Can the next person proceed?

Good reporting therefore improves accountability, task execution, client service, team coordination, leadership visibility, follow-through, standards compliance, problem-solving, decision-making, and operational efficiency.
The purpose of reporting is not simply to produce messages. The purpose is to make sure the right information reaches the right person at the right time so the next appropriate action can happen.

sections.title: 2. The Reporting Mindset
paragraphs: The therapist's mindset should be: "If my work affects another person, that person should not have to chase me to know what happened."
Reporting is responsibility. It is not an optional administrative activity.
Reporting is not betrayal. Reporting a concern about a colleague does not automatically mean attacking the colleague.
Reporting is not gossip. It has a clear recipient and purpose.
Reporting is not complaining. A good report helps somebody understand, decide, review, correct, or act.
Reporting should be proactive. Do not wait until someone asks "Have you done it?" when you were expected to report completion yourself.

sections.title: 3. Who Should Receive a Report?
paragraphs: Reports should be directed to the appropriate leader or operational channel, depending on the matter.
This may include Therapist Guide (TG), Lead Therapist (LT), Supervisor (SP), Client Manager (CM), Staff Manager (SM), and Manager.
The therapist should learn to understand: Who assigned the task? Who supervises this responsibility? Who needs the information? Who has authority to review or make the next decision?
Not every report needs to go directly to the Manager. Reporting should follow the appropriate leadership structure unless the matter is urgent, serious, unresolved, or involves the immediate leader.

sections.title: 4. Reporting on the Appropriate WhatsApp Wall
paragraphs: Zura Spa uses designated WhatsApp groups/walls/channels to maintain operational visibility.
Where a task or routine is expected to be updated on a particular wall, the therapist must report it there.
Examples may include massage/session update wall, task wall, staff/operations wall, stock or supplies wall, leadership wall, and other approved operational groups.
A report sent privately to one colleague does not necessarily replace an update that was required on the designated wall.

For example: If a task was assigned through the Task Wall and completion is expected there, saying privately "I told Thr. Jane that I finished it" does not mean the required completion report has been made.
REPORT WHERE THE TEAM EXPECTS THE REPORT TO BE. This ensures that the relevant people have the same visibility.

sections.title: 5. Reporting Is Part of Task Completion
paragraphs: At Zura Spa, task completion generally follows: ASSIGNED → UNDERSTOOD → EXECUTED → COMPLETION REPORT → REVIEW → CLOSED.
The therapist should not stop at "I have done it." The next question is: "Who needs to know that I have done it?"
Where reporting is required, the task remains operationally incomplete until the report has been given.

sections.title: 6. Task Completion Report
paragraphs: A Task Completion Report is the update given immediately after an assigned task has been completed.
Its purpose is to tell the appropriate leader, the person who assigned the task, the relevant team, and the appropriate WhatsApp wall that the task has been completed and what the outcome was.
A good Task Completion Report answers: What task was completed? When was it completed? What was the outcome? Was everything completed as expected? Is anything still pending? Is review required?

sections.title: Task Completion Report Example
paragraphs: Instead of "Done," prefer:
"SM, Room 2 preparation completed. Bed laid, fresh towels replaced, massage oil restocked and equipment checked. Room is ready for use."
"LT, Massage Assessment practice completed with Thr. Jane. Pressure control and synchronization were practised. Awaiting your review."
"Stock count completed and posted on the Stock Wall. Massage oil is low; 3 bottles remain."
The report should give enough information to make the status clear.

sections.title: 7. Task Review Report
paragraphs: A Task Review Report is different from the completion report.
The completion report says: "The task has been done." The review report says: "The work has been checked, and this is what was found."
A review may be carried out by TG, LT, SP, CM, SM, Manager, or another authorized reviewer depending on the responsibility.
A Task Review Report may confirm: task completed correctly, task completed but needs correction, task partly completed, task failed standard, additional action required, or task accepted and closed.

sections.title: Task Review Report Example
paragraphs: "Task Review — Room 2 checked. Room is clean and properly prepared. Task accepted and closed."
"Task Review — Fresh sheets and towels are ready, but massage gun was not cleaned. Thr. Jane to correct and update once completed."
"Assessment Review — Technique improved, but pressure control and co-therapist synchronization require additional practice. Reassessment required."
The review report should make the next step obvious.

sections.title: 8. Completion Does Not Always Mean Acceptance
paragraphs: This distinction is important.
A therapist may complete a task and report "Task completed." But where the task requires review, leadership may determine "Correction required."
COMPLETED BY THERAPIST ≠ AUTOMATICALLY APPROVED BY REVIEWER.
Where review is required, the task is closed only after: COMPLETION → REVIEW → CORRECTION IF NECESSARY → CONFIRMATION.

sections.title: 9. Progress Report
paragraphs: Some tasks take time. A therapist should not remain silent from assignment until completion if leadership reasonably needs progress visibility.
A Progress Report should explain current stage, what has been completed, what remains, whether the task is on schedule, and whether there is a blocker.
Example: "SP, stock count is about 70% complete. Towels and massage supplies are done; cleaning materials remain. I expect completion by 4 PM."
Progress reports prevent unnecessary chasing.

sections.title: 10. Blocker Report
paragraphs: Where a therapist cannot proceed, the therapist should report the blocker early. Do not wait until the task deadline and then say "I couldn't do it."
A proper blocker report explains: What you are trying to do. What is stopping you. What you have already tried. What assistance you need.
Example: "SM, I cannot complete the room setup because there are no clean towels available. I have checked the linen area and informed housekeeping. Please advise."
A blocker may not be your fault. Failing to report the blocker can still become your accountability issue.

sections.title: 11. Incident or Mistake Report
paragraphs: If something goes wrong — property is damaged, a mistake occurs, client experience is affected, wrong information is given, stock is lost, a routine is missed, or an incident occurs — report promptly.
The report should explain: What happened? When? Who was involved where relevant? What was your own role? What action has already been taken? What assistance is required?
Do not wait for management to discover the incident independently.

sections.title: 12. Reporting Standard Violations
paragraphs: If a therapist observes another therapist repeatedly or seriously flouting Zura Spa standards, the matter should be reported appropriately.
The purpose is not "I want Thr. Jane to get into trouble." The purpose is "There is a standard issue that needs correction."

The therapist should communicate what was observed, when it occurred, which standard is involved, whether the person was reminded where appropriate, whether the issue is recurring, and whether it affected a client or the team.
Avoid exaggeration or assigning motives you cannot know.

sections.title: 13. Client-Related Reports
paragraphs: Important information about clients should be communicated through the appropriate channel.

Examples include client complaint, client request, client discomfort, client asks to speak with CM, client wants additional service, client requests water, client indicates intention to tip, client behaviour raises concern, session has been paused, client is preparing to leave, and important client feedback.
This works together with the Massage Task & Session Update Standard.
If another person needs the information to properly support the client, communicate it.

sections.title: 14. Stock Reports
paragraphs: Therapists should report low stock, missing stock, damaged stock, unexplained differences, items approaching exhaustion, completed stock counts, and items requiring replacement.
Do not wait until an item completely finishes.
Example: "SM, stock update: massage oil has 3 bottles remaining. At current usage this may not be sufficient for the next few days. Restock required."
This gives management time to act.

sections.title: 15. Company Property Reports
paragraphs: Any damage, fault, malfunction, loss, or unsafe condition should be reported promptly.
Example: "SP, Massage Gun 2 stopped working during testing. It has been removed from use and kept at the equipment desk. No visible physical damage."
This is better than leaving it for another therapist to discover during a client session.

sections.title: 16. The Reporting Procedure
paragraphs: When reporting, therapists should follow this process.

sections.title: Step 1 — Identify What Needs to Be Reported
paragraphs: Ask: Does this information affect a client, task, leader, colleague, stock, property, standard, or next action? If yes, report where appropriate.

sections.title: Step 2 — Identify the Appropriate Recipient
paragraphs: Ask: Who is responsible for this matter? Choose the appropriate TG → LT → SP → CM → SM → Manager as applicable.

sections.title: Step 3 — Identify the Correct Channel
paragraphs: Determine whether the report should be on the appropriate WhatsApp wall, directly to a leader, both on the wall and directly to a leader, or recorded through another approved process.

sections.title: Step 4 — Report Promptly
paragraphs: Do not wait unnecessarily. A report that comes after the opportunity to act has passed may have little value.

sections.title: Step 5 — Report the Facts
paragraphs: Explain what actually happened. Separate FACT from OPINION from ASSUMPTION.

sections.title: Step 6 — State the Current Status
paragraphs: Examples: Completed. Pending. Blocked. Requires review. Requires correction. Escalated. Awaiting approval.

sections.title: Step 7 — State What Is Needed Next
paragraphs: Examples: "Awaiting LT review." "CM please assist." "Restock required." "Task completed and ready for inspection."

sections.title: Step 8 — Respond to Review
paragraphs: If the reviewer requests correction: correct it, update again, and do not disappear after the first report.

sections.title: Step 9 — Close the Loop
paragraphs: The reporting cycle should end when the task or issue is properly closed.
REPORT → RESPONSE → ACTION → CONFIRMATION → CLOSURE.

sections.title: 17. How a Good Report Should Sound
paragraphs: A good Zura Spa report should be clear, brief, specific, accurate, timely, professional, and actionable.

The reader understands what happened. Do not bury the important information in unnecessary details. Say what was done or what went wrong. Do not exaggerate. Send it while the information can still be useful. Avoid insults or emotional language. Make the next action clear.

sections.title: 18. Reporting vs Gossip
paragraphs: REPORTING goes to someone who needs the information, has an operational purpose, uses relevant facts, seeks action, review, correction, support, or accountability, and usually stops once the issue is resolved.

GOSSIP goes to people who do not need the information, often seeks reaction rather than resolution, contains opinions, assumptions, or unnecessary private details, and continues even when there is nothing useful to be done.
The test is: "Can this person do something useful with the information I am giving them?" If not, ask whether the conversation is necessary.

sections.title: 19. What the Opposite Looks Like
paragraphs: The opposite of good reporting includes several patterns.

sections.title: Completing a Task Silently
paragraphs: The task is done but nobody who needs the information knows.

sections.title: Waiting to Be Chased
paragraphs: Leadership must repeatedly ask: "Have you done it?"

sections.title: Saying Only "Done"
paragraphs: Saying only "Done" when the outcome or status needs explanation.

sections.title: Reporting in the Wrong Place
paragraphs: The therapist privately tells one friend when the update belongs on the operational wall.

sections.title: Reporting Too Late
paragraphs: The information arrives after the opportunity to solve the problem has passed.

sections.title: Giving Incomplete Reports
paragraphs: Important facts are omitted.

sections.title: Giving Biased Reports
paragraphs: Information is deliberately framed to make one person look good or bad.

sections.title: Reporting Emotionally
paragraphs: The therapist focuses on anger rather than facts.

sections.title: Failing to Report Mistakes
paragraphs: Management discovers the problem from someone else.

sections.title: Reporting Completion Falsely
paragraphs: The therapist claims a task has been done when it has not. This is a serious accountability issue.

sections.title: 20. Why Zura Spa Will Not Tolerate Poor Reporting
paragraphs: Poor reporting causes operational blindness. Leadership cannot manage what it cannot see. The team cannot coordinate around information it does not have.

Zura Spa therefore cannot normalize silent task completion, repeatedly needing to chase updates, hiding mistakes, late reporting, false reports, misleading reports, reporting to the wrong people, gossip instead of proper reporting, failing to communicate blockers, or claiming completion before work is actually done.
Reporting is part of accountability.

sections.title: 21. Impact of Poor Reporting on the Team
paragraphs: Poor reporting affects more than the therapist involved. It can cause duplicate work, missed tasks, confusion, leaders repeatedly chasing information, delayed client service, stock shortages, missed client requests, undetected mistakes, unnecessary conflict, poor handovers, and micromanagement.
When people report consistently, leadership can trust the system. When people do not report, leaders begin physically checking everything themselves.
GOOD REPORTING CREATES TRUST. POOR REPORTING CREATES MICROMANAGEMENT.

sections.title: 22. Impact on the Client
paragraphs: The client may never see the report. But they experience the consequence.

Water request reported immediately — client receives water. Request not reported — client waits. Client concern reported — CM can intervene. Concern hidden — client leaves dissatisfied. Massage completion reported — front desk prepares for departure. No report — client arrives downstairs while nobody is prepared.
Internal communication directly affects external service.

sections.title: 23. What Therapists Should Do
list: Report task completion without being chased.
Give completion reports after assigned tasks.
Report serious or repeated standard violations.
Follow up until the issue or task is properly closed.

sections.title: 24. What Therapists Should Not Do
list: Complete a task and remain silent when reporting is required.
Wait for leaders to ask repeatedly.
Say "done" when more information is necessary.
Report completion before the task is actually complete.
Tell random colleagues instead of the correct leader.
Report on the wrong wall deliberately.
Gossip about an issue instead of escalating it.
Add assumptions as though they were facts.
Hide information to protect a friend.
Ignore feedback after a task review.
Refuse to correct a task that did not meet standard.
Assume that posting once means the responsibility is finished when follow-up is required.

sections.title: 25. Reporting and Accountability
paragraphs: At Zura Spa: Task completed + reported properly = responsibility. Task completed + reviewed + accepted = closure. Blocker identified + reported early = professionalism. Mistake made + reported honestly = accountability. Standard breach observed + responsibly reported = protecting the standard.

But: Task completed + no update = incomplete communication. Repeatedly requiring leaders to chase updates = performance concern. False completion report = serious accountability concern. Knowingly hiding a serious incident = serious conduct concern. Knowingly giving a false report against another person = serious disciplinary concern.

sections.title: 26. The Zura Spa Reporting Standard
paragraphs: DO → UPDATE → REPORT → REVIEW → CORRECT → CONFIRM → CLOSE

Every therapist should ask: What was I asked to do? Have I actually completed it? Who assigned it? Who needs to know? Which WhatsApp wall should receive the update? Have I given the Task Completion Report? Does the task require review? Has the Task Review Report been given? Is there a correction I still need to make? Has the task actually been closed?

DON'T LEAVE MANAGEMENT GUESSING. DON'T WAIT TO BE CHASED. DON'T CONFUSE DOING THE TASK WITH COMPLETING THE COMMUNICATION. DON'T HIDE MISTAKES. DON'T GOSSIP ABOUT WHAT SHOULD BE REPORTED. REPORT TO THE RIGHT LEADER. REPORT ON THE RIGHT WALL. REPORT COMPLETION. ALLOW REVIEW. CORRECT WHERE NECESSARY. CLOSE THE LOOP.
A responsible therapist does not only do the work. A responsible therapist makes sure the right people know what was done, what happened, what remains, and what needs to happen next.
REPORT TO INFORM. REPORT TO ACCOUNT. REPORT TO IMPROVE. REPORT TO PROTECT THE STANDARD.

remember: Doing the task is not enough — report completion to the right person on the right channel, allow review, and close the loop.
